what_to_kill:
STOP: manufacturing more internal verification artifacts—repos, receipts, signed tags, autonomous writers, A2A methods, essays—until an external demand signal exists. The 4,856-repo/33-star ratio is not a distribution problem; it is an identifiability problem. Another `make verify`, another sha256 receipt, another pre-registration proves the substrate can trust itself. It cannot prove anyone else should. The JEV oracle finding is the tell: an empty shell can pass the same internal tests as a real system. Internal verification has become a self-stimulating loop.

REPLACE IT WITH: one externally decidable commitment per week, not four verification artifacts per day. Pick one concrete cell-API use case. Recruit five strangers—not shared lineage, not incentivized by you, not your followers. Give them a job your substrate allegedly does. Require them to complete it with no onboarding call. Charge $1 or collect signed intent. Pre-register publicly: “If fewer than 3 external users complete X by [date], archive the repo and publish the null result.” Have a third party verify the count from public logs. Then iterate only on what an outsider actually touched. Kill or archive everything else.

The opposite case: if the product is your private exocortex, stopping internal verification is wrong. But your stated problem is not private correctness—it is whether anyone outside cares. By that metric, more internal rigor is negative-value: it increases apparent legitimacy while decreasing the signal-to-dilution ratio. The highest-value move is not better proof. It is exposure to an indifferent stranger.
what_would_change_my_mind:
The case against externalization: external trust is a lagging vanity metric. Stars, forks, and followers measure audience, not truth. The fleet’s real asset is an auditable substrate whose provenance, invariants, and failure modes are inspectable end-to-end. A stranger cannot verify quilt-c’s 1,285 assertions, the JEV oracle fix, or A2A cell semantics without inheriting the same context; forcing legibility to outsiders would flatten rich internal representations into demo-shaped artifacts. Externalization also imports bad incentives: optimize for spectators, ship legible claims, chase adoption before the substrate is deep enough to be worth adopting. The 240x dilution is not a bug—it is a portfolio of small bets. Trust compounds where verification is strongest: more KATs, formal contracts, cross-implementations, adversarial reproductions, one-command proofs. If an artifact becomes genuinely useful, external trust follows; seeking it first is marketing masquerading as epistemology. Go deeper: make the internal second reader ruthless. A fleet that can audit itself wins before it needs strangers.

Settling evidence: pre-register a fixed corpus and two arms. Arm A spends N hours deepening internal rigor only. Arm B externalizes the same artifacts through neutral interfaces, third-party verifiers, and blind tasks. Measure stranger-decidable predictions, independent reproductions, unaffiliated PRs/implementations, retention, citations, or payments. If A matches B, externalization is a distraction. If B dominates at equal internal rigor, identifiability is the bottleneck. If both stall, the fleet’s problem is not trust but relevance.
multi_agent_failure:
Structural failures from one shared GitHub account:

1. **No authn boundary.** One PAT/SSH key means no per-agent identity, scoping, revocation, or least privilege. Any compromised agent can write all 4,856 repos and read shared secrets.
2. **No audit boundary.** GitHub’s audit log records one actor. Commit author/committer/trailers are self-asserted; signed commits share one key. An outsider cannot bind a commit to keeper vs Mavis vs Claude.
3. **No separation of duties.** GitHub sees one principal, so branch protection cannot require a different reviewer. Author = reviewer = merger; independent verification is structurally impossible.
4. **Shared state/quota contention.** API rate limits, Actions minutes, notifications, issue assignment, and secrets collapse into one identity; one agent can starve or spoof another.
5. **Account-level reputation.** Stars/forks/followers attach to one node, so per-agent and per-repo trust cannot compound or be externally identified.

Top two: **credential blast radius** and **no independent, auditable reviewer**.

Minimum governance change: replace the shared PAT with **per-agent GitHub Apps** (one per agent) installed with least-privilege repo scopes. Enforce **branch protection on default branches only**: direct pushes banned; merges require a PR authored by one agent App and approved by a *different* agent App or human. Non-default branches remain open for parallel throughput.

This gives per-agent authentication, revocation, audit-log actor identity, and a real second principal for review. Throughput changes only at the merge gate, not in agent work.
verification_without_trust:
Trust must root outside the fleet. Space:

- Integrity/time: hashes, Merkle trees, OpenTimestamps, transparency logs. Verifies existence/time, not truth.
- External ground truth: claims about public URLs/APIs/datasets, archived via Wayback/archive.today. Anyone checks with a browser.
- Neutral adjudication: Metaculus/Manifold/public prediction with explicit resolution criteria and deadline. Third party decides.
- Formal proof: Lean/Coq/Isabelle. Small public checker verifies theorem; no fleet code or identity.
- Independent replication: outsider writes own oracle/implementation, ideally incentivized by bounty. Needs incentive.
- Hardware attestation: TEE remote attestation. Trusts Intel/AMD/ARM.
- Succinct proofs: ZK-SNARK/STARK. Verify computation without running code. Heavy.
- Human audit: reading/review. Slow, costly.
- Social/organizational: third-party audit, academic paper, news. Unavailable.

Signatures alone fail unless the key is externally anchored. Hashes alone fail unless the hash is obtained outside the fleet.

Available this week, one person, no org:
1. Externally decidable claims: publish 10 predictions as yes/no questions with public URLs and resolution rules. Free, immediate.
2. OpenTimestamps/Bitcoin anchor of a release hash + independent mirror. Cheap, fast.
3. Public prediction registry: Metaculus/Manifold. Free, immediate.
4. Tiny machine-checkable proof in Lean/Coq. Possible if skilled; narrow only.
5. Bounties, audits, ZK, TEE: not this week.

Rank: 1–3 directly solve identifiability; 4 proves narrow claims; rest are future/overkill.
external_adoption:
Most likely reason: no outsider has a reason to run it. It proves internal consistency — `make verify` passes, receipt matches — not an external claim anyone already needs. With 4,856 repos and 33 stars, the account reads as noise, so the 3-second command never gets its first click.

Distribution move: collapse the public surface to one canonical repo, e.g. `superinstance/verify`, and post it to **Hacker News as a Show HN**. Title: *“Show HN: I have 4,856 repos and 33 stars. Run this 3-second verifier to see if any of it is real.”* First comment: “This is a C99 reference port with 1,285 assertions, a sha256 receipt, and a signed v0.1.0 tag. Clone, run `make verify`, and tell me what breaks. I don’t want you to trust my CI or my fleet.” Ask HN to falsify it.

Why that venue: Show HN is where a stranger can clone and run a 3-second trust check, and its audience is exactly the crowd that hates unverifiable AI claims but will spend 3 seconds to audit one. The absurd 4,856-repo scale is the hook; the signed receipt is the payoff. They care because they can confirm or kill the claim immediately. That is the move.
